sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** The TCP/IP model is a four-layer networking framework — Link, Internet, Transport, Application — that describes how the real internet moves data, collapsing the OSI model's seven layers into the four that actually ship in production operating systems.
The TCP/IP model (sometimes called the DoD or ARPANET model) predates OSI and is what every modern operating system actually implements. Where OSI is a teaching abstraction, TCP/IP is the running code. Its four layers, bottom-up, are Link (Ethernet, Wi-Fi, ARP — what OSI calls L1+L2), Internet (IP, ICMP — OSI L3), Transport (TCP, UDP, QUIC — OSI L4), and Application (HTTP, DNS, gRPC, SSH — OSI L5+L6+L7). The collapse is honest: real implementations rarely have a distinct Session or Presentation layer; the application itself opens a socket (which is the session) and serializes data as JSON or Protobuf (which is the presentation). The model is named for its two most important protocols — Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) at L4 and Internet Protocol (IP) at L3 — and the entire web stack runs on top of those two building blocks.

The crown jewel of the Transport layer is TCP, a connection-oriented, reliable, in-order byte stream. TCP establishes a connection with the famous three-way handshake: the client sends SYN with a random sequence number `x`; the server replies SYN-ACK with its own sequence `y` and an acknowledgment `x+1`; the client replies ACK with `y+1`. From this point both sides can send data, with every byte acknowledged and retransmitted if lost. Connection teardown is symmetric: each side sends FIN when done sending, the other ACKs, and the closing side waits in TIME-WAIT for two maximum segment lifetimes (typically 60–120 seconds) to absorb stray duplicate packets. TCP also implements flow control via a sliding window advertised by the receiver, and congestion control via algorithms like Reno/Cubic that use slow start (exponential window growth), congestion avoidance (linear growth), and AIMD (additive increase, multiplicative decrease) on packet loss. These mechanisms are why a single TCP connection can saturate a 100-Gbps transcontinental link without overwhelming it.

Why does this matter in real systems? Because almost every production data path is a TCP connection, and TCP's behavior shapes your application's latency, throughput, and failure modes. Kafka is the canonical example: every Kafka producer, consumer, and broker communicates over long-lived TCP connections, and Kafka brokers reuse the same TCP connection for many topic-partition fetches to amortize the handshake cost. At LinkedIn scale (7 trillion messages per day), the choice to use raw TCP rather than HTTP matters enormously — every saved SYN/FIN cycle is billions of operations, and TCP's flow control prevents a slow consumer from being overwhelmed by a fast producer. HTTP/2 similarly multiplexes many logical streams over a single TCP connection, eliminating head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer (though not at the TCP layer, which is what motivated HTTP/3 over QUIC). Understanding TCP is understanding the floor of what distributed systems can achieve.

Real-world: Netflix's Open Connect content delivery network pushes petabytes per second over TCP between origin and edge appliances, and they tune TCP's congestion control aggressively (BBR instead of Cubic) to push throughput on long-fat pipes where Reno/Cubic back off too aggressively. AWS's internal Nitro network uses custom TCP tuning to hit single-digit-microsecond latency between EC2 instances. gRPC defaults to HTTP/2 over TCP, and its connection pooling strategy is fundamentally a TCP-keepalive strategy. On the failure side, the TCP TIME-WAIT state is a notorious production issue: a load test that opens millions of short-lived connections can exhaust ephemeral ports (typically 28,000 available on Linux) and bring a service to its knees. The fix is either keep-alive (reuse connections) or `SO_REUSEADDR` plus careful tuning of `tcp_tw_reuse`.

The trade-off: TCP offers reliability and ordering at the cost of latency and head-of-line blocking. A single lost packet stalls all bytes behind it until retransmission succeeds, which is catastrophic for latency-sensitive workloads like voice, video, or gaming. UDP skips all of this — no handshake, no reliability, no ordering — and pushes those concerns to the application. QUIC (which underpins HTTP/3) is essentially "TCP's reliability re-implemented on UDP" so that streams can be multiplexed without head-of-line blocking at the transport layer; a lost packet stalls one QUIC stream, not the whole connection. The other classic pitfall is the Nagle algorithm (RFC 896), which delays small packets to coalesce them — great for keystrokes over telnet, terrible for latency-sensitive RPCs, which is why most production systems set `TCP_NODELAY`. Knowing when TCP's reliability is worth its latency cost, and when to escape to UDP or QUIC, is one of the most impactful architecture decisions you can make.

TCP/IP connects to every other networking concept: HTTP (Topic 3) and HTTPS (Topic 4) ride on top of TCP (or QUIC), DNS uses both UDP and TCP, and message queues like Kafka, RabbitMQ, and Pulsar all use TCP under the hood. It also connects back to Phase 1: TCP's flow control is a real-world example of backpressure, and AIMD congestion control is a distributed-systems feedback loop you'll see echoed in token-bucket rate limiters and adaptive load shedding. Latency budgets (Topic 8) must account for TCP handshake RTT and slow-start ramp-up; throughput targets (Topic 9) are bounded by the TCP window size and BDP.

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server

    Note over C,S: TCP 3-way handshake (connection setup)
    C->>S: SYN seq=x
    S->>C: SYN-ACK seq=y ack=x+1
    C->>S: ACK seq=x+1 ack=y+1

    Note over C,S: Data transfer (with ACKs)
    C->>S: DATA seq=x+1 len=100
    S->>C: ACK ack=x+101
    S->>C: DATA seq=y+1 len=200
    C->>S: ACK ack=y+201

    Note over C,S: Graceful close (4-way)
    C->>S: FIN seq=x+101
    S->>C: ACK ack=x+102
    S->>C: FIN seq=y+201
    C->>S: ACK ack=y+202
    Note over C: TIME-WAIT 2*MSL (~60-120s)
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
TCP/IP Model               OSI Model               Example Protocols
+---------------------+    +---------------------+   +----------------+
| Application         | <- | L7 Application       |   | HTTP, gRPC,    |
|                     |    | L6 Presentation      |   | DNS, SSH, MQTT |
|                     |    | L5 Session           |   |                |
+---------------------+    +---------------------+   +----------------+
| Transport           | <- | L4 Transport         |   | TCP, UDP, QUIC |
+---------------------+    +---------------------+   +----------------+
| Internet            | <- | L3 Network           |   | IPv4, IPv6,    |
|                     |    |                     |   | ICMP, BGP      |
+---------------------+    +---------------------+   +----------------+
| Link                | <- | L2 Data Link         |   | Ethernet, ARP, |
|                     |    | L1 Physical          |   | Wi-Fi, VXLAN   |
+---------------------+    +---------------------+   +----------------+

TCP Congestion Window over time (slow start + AIMD):
cwnd
  |                          /\      /\      /\
  |                         /  \    /  \    /  \    <-- additive increase
  |             /\         /    \  /    \  /    \
  |            /  \       /      \/      \/      \
  |           /    \     /   (loss: multiplicative decrease)
  |          /      \   /
  |   /\    /        \ /
  |  /  \  /
  | /    \/  <-- slow start (exponential)
  |/
  +--------------------------------------------------> RTT
```

### Walkthrough
1. The client picks a random sequence number `x` and sends SYN. The server allocates state, picks `y`, and replies SYN-ACK. The client's final ACK means both sides have agreed on initial sequence numbers and can begin sending data.
2. During data transfer, every byte has a sequence number; the receiver ACKs the next expected byte. If an ACK doesn't arrive within RTO (retransmit timeout), the sender retransmits. Congestion control grows `cwnd` exponentially in slow start, then linearly in congestion avoidance, halving it on loss (AIMD).
3. To close, each side sends FIN when done transmitting. The other side ACKs the FIN, sends its own FIN, and the initiator enters TIME-WAIT for 2*MSL to absorb any delayed duplicate packets before releasing the port.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
"""
TCP server + client demonstrating the 3-way handshake and graceful close.

Run twice in two terminals:
    Terminal 1:  python3 tcp_demo.py server
    Terminal 2:  python3 tcp_demo.py client

What to observe in `tcpdump -i lo -n port 50007`:
    SYN           client -> server   seq=x
    SYN-ACK       server -> client   seq=y  ack=x+1
    ACK           client -> server   seq=x+1 ack=y+1
    PSH-ACK data  both ways
    FIN-ACK       four-way teardown
"""

import socket
import sys
import threading
import time

HOST = "127.0.0.1"
PORT = 50007

def server() -> None:
    with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM) as srv:
        # Allow quick restart without TIME-WAIT pain in dev.
        srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
        srv.bind((HOST, PORT))
        srv.listen(1)
        print(f"[server] listening on {HOST}:{PORT} (waiting for SYN)...")
        conn, addr = srv.accept()
        with conn:
            print(f"[server] SYN-ACK sent, ACK received from {addr} -- handshake complete")
            # Receive a chunk of data (TCP is a byte stream, not message-oriented).
            data = conn.recv(1024)
            print(f"[server] received {len(data)} bytes: {data!r}")
            # Send a reply, then close cleanly.
            conn.sendall(b"hello from server")
            print("[server] sending FIN to close my write side")
        # `with conn` exit closes the socket -> kernel sends FIN.
    print("[server] socket closed; kernel may hold TIME-WAIT for 2*MSL")

def client() -> None:
    with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM) as s:
        # Disable Nagle so the small request goes out immediately.
        s.setsockopt(socket.IPPROTO_TCP, socket.TCP_NODELAY, 1)
        print(f"[client] sending SYN to {HOST}:{PORT} ...")
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        s.connect((HOST, PORT))     # <-- 3-way handshake happens here
        t1 = time.perf_counter()
        print(f"[client] handshake complete in {(t1-t0)*1000:.2f} ms")

        s.sendall(b"ping")
        print("[client] sent 'ping'")

        reply = s.recv(1024)
        print(f"[client] received reply: {reply!r}")
        # Graceful close: kernel sends FIN, waits for peer FIN, then ACK.
    print("[client] socket closed (FIN sent)")

def main() -> None:
    if len(sys.argv) != 2 or sys.argv[1] not in ("server", "client"):
        print("usage: python3 tcp_demo.py [server|client]")
        sys.exit(1)

    if sys.argv[1] == "client":
        client()
    else:
        # Run server in-process so the snippet is self-contained.
        threading.Thread(target=server, daemon=True).start()
        time.sleep(0.3)   # let the server bind() first
        client()
        time.sleep(0.5)   # let server's TIME-WAIT log flush

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

quiz.explanation: Slow start is the first phase of TCP congestion control. The sender starts with cwnd (congestion window) of 1–10 segments and doubles it every RTT until it hits the slow-start threshold (ssthresh) or detects loss.

quiz.question: What is the difference between TCP flow control and congestion control?
options: Slow start is the first phase of TCP congestion control.
In congestion avoidance mode, TCP grows cwnd by 1 segment per RTT (additive increase) and halves it on loss (multiplicative decrease).
TIME-WAIT is the state entered by the side that closes first, after sending its final ACK to the peer's FIN.
Congestion control, in contrast, is the sender's own estimate of network capacity and is implemented entirely on the sender side without any header field — the sender probes by growing…
quiz.explanation: Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects the network. Flow control uses the sliding window advertised in the TCP header (the win field) to tell the sender how much free buffer the receiver has. If the receiver's socket buffer fills because the application is slow to read, the window shrinks to zero, and the sender pauses until a window update arrives.

quiz.question: Why does TCP have a TIME-WAIT state, and why is it a common production problem?
options: Three reasons: amortized handshake cost, finer flow control, and protocol efficiency.
Multiplayer games need low-latency state updates where stale data is worse than missing data — exactly the workload TCP was designed against.
This is almost certainly TCP retransmit timeout (RTO) behavior on a lost packet.
TIME-WAIT is the state entered by the side that closes first, after sending its final ACK to the peer's FIN.
quiz.explanation: TIME-WAIT is the state entered by the side that closes first, after sending its final ACK to the peer's FIN. It lasts 2×MSL (typically 60–120 seconds) to absorb any duplicate packets from the closed connection that might still be wandering the network — without it, a delayed FIN retransmit could spuriously close a newly-reopened connection using the same 4-tuple.

quiz.explanation: In congestion avoidance mode, TCP grows cwnd by 1 segment per RTT (additive increase) and halves it on loss (multiplicative decrease). The classic fairness argument: if N TCP connections share a bottleneck, the one using more than its fair share will experience more loss and back off multiplicatively, while the one using less will keep growing additively.
